title: Hyderabad's Forest & Fire Festival Puts India's Forgotten Tribal Cuisine on the Table
excerpt: Chef Harshita Kakwani's 10-day culinary celebration at Novotel Hyderabad draws on Central India's indigenous food traditions, featuring dishes made with mahua, wild mushrooms, and bamboo.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The Forest & Fire festival runs from July 17 to 26 at Novotel Hyderabad.
  • Chef Harshita Kakwani curates a menu featuring indigenous Central Indian dishes.
  • Dishes include Mahua Mushroom Bao and Hay-Smoked Fish, highlighting foraged ingredients.
  • The grand dinner buffet costs INR 2,799, with thali options starting at INR 1,200.
  • The festival promotes awareness of India's diverse tribal food traditions.
Culinary Highlights of Forest & Fire
›Mahua Mushroom Bao: Wild mushrooms with mahua flowers.
›Hay-Smoked Fish: Ancient preservation technique.
›Patrapoda Jackfruit: Wrapped in sal leaves.
›Junglee Mutton: Traditional tribal preparation.
›Bamboo Bhurji: Made with foraged bamboo shoots.
  • The Forest & Fire food festival runs July 17–26 at Novotel Hyderabad Convention Centre, featuring a grand dinner buffet, culinary masterclass, and bar takeover.
  • Chef Harshita Kakwani, a food researcher specializing in indigenous Indian cuisine, has curated a menu drawing on Central India's tribal food traditions and wood-fire cooking techniques.
  • Dishes include Mahua Mushroom Bao, Hay-Smoked Fish, Patrapoda Jackfruit, Junglee Mutton, and Bamboo Bhurji — using foraged and seasonal ingredients largely absent from mainstream restaurant menus.
  • The grand dinner buffet is priced at INR 2,799 per person, with vegetarian and non-vegetarian thali options starting at INR 1,200.

Novotel Hyderabad Convention Centre has launched Forest & Fire, a 10-day food festival that brings India's indigenous tribal cuisine to a fine-dining setting. Running from July 17 to 26 at the hotel's Food Exchange and Permit To Grill restaurants, the event is curated by Chef Harshita Kakwani, a food researcher and culinary storyteller known for documenting and reviving the food traditions of India's forest-dwelling communities.

The festival's menu reads like an inventory of ingredients that most urban Indian diners have never encountered on a restaurant plate. Mahua Mushroom Bao pairs wild mushrooms with the dried flowers of the mahua tree, a staple of Adivasi communities across Central India. Hay-Smoked Fish uses an ancient preservation technique. Patrapoda Jackfruit borrows from Odisha's tribal cooking tradition of wrapping food in sal leaves. Kala Mutton Taco, Saoji Chicken, Junglee Mutton, and Bamboo Bhurji round out a menu that also includes traditional grains, regional breads, and desserts made from forest produce.

From Forest Floor to Fine Dining

Chef Kakwani's work sits at the intersection of food research, sustainability, and gastronomy. She has spent years traveling through Central India's forest regions, documenting the cooking practices of indigenous communities — knowledge systems that have been passed down through generations but remain largely invisible in India's restaurant industry.

Her culinary philosophy centers on seasonal sourcing, forgotten ingredients, and wood-fire cooking methods that predate the modern kitchen. At Forest & Fire, that translates to dishes built around rustic spices, foraged greens, and smoke — the elemental flavours of India's forests, presented in a contemporary dining format.

Beyond the Buffet

The festival extends past the dinner table. On July 18, Chef Kakwani hosts "The Craft," a culinary masterclass running from 1:00 PM to 3:00 PM, priced at INR 1,500 per person. Participants will learn the stories, techniques, and ingredients behind indigenous Indian cooking, with hands-on preparation of signature dishes from the festival menu.

On July 25, the hotel presents "The Pour," a bar takeover at Permit To Grill from 6:30 PM to 8:30 PM. The hotel's bar team collaborates with Chef Kakwani to create cocktails and beverages made with local and forest-derived ingredients — a drinks menu designed to complement the festival's food.

The main event, the Forest & Fire Grand Dinner Buffet, runs nightly from 7:00 PM to 11:00 PM. Pricing sits at INR 2,799 per person for the full buffet, with a vegetarian thali at INR 1,200 and a non-vegetarian thali at INR 1,400. The dining spaces will feature nature-inspired décor, live music, and themed ambience meant to evoke India's forest landscapes.

Why Tribal Cuisine Matters Now

India's indigenous food traditions have long occupied the margins of the country's culinary conversation, overshadowed by the regional cuisines of its major cities. But a growing movement of chefs and food researchers is working to change that, arguing that tribal cooking holds lessons for sustainable eating, biodiversity preservation, and nutritional diversity.

Chef Kakwani is part of this wave. Her approach — grounding fine-dining menus in the foodways of Adivasi communities — pushes back against the notion that India's culinary heritage begins and ends with biryani, butter chicken, and dosas. The ingredients she champions — mahua flowers, wild bamboo shoots, sal leaves, foraged mushrooms — are staples for millions of tribal Indians but remain foreign to most restaurant kitchens.

A Broader Trend in Hyderabad

The festival reflects Hyderabad's emergence as one of India's more adventurous food cities. Novotel Hyderabad Convention Centre has built a track record of collaborating with guest chefs to bring regional cuisines to the city, and Forest & Fire is its most ambitious effort to spotlight indigenous food culture.

For diaspora Indians watching from abroad, the festival is a reminder that India's food landscape is far more diverse than what typically makes it onto international menus. The tribal cuisines of Central India — built on foraged ingredients, fermentation, and fire — represent a culinary tradition that predates recorded history and is only now getting the mainstream attention it deserves.

Forest & Fire runs through July 26 at Novotel Hyderabad Convention Centre.
